newsitem.title: USA: Daschle criticizes Republicans' common tax stance.
newsitem.headline: Daschle criticizes Republicans' common tax stance.

text.p: A top Senate Democrat on Wednesday sharply criticised the Republicans' common tax stance as talks between the White House and Congress were scheduled to resume on balanced-budget legislation.

Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle told reporters that the compromise worked out among the Republicans who control both houses of Congress was unacceptable to Democrats and called its inclusion of capital gains indexing a "nonstarter."
"The bad news is they produced a bill that only Republicans can support. So now negotiations must begin in earnest," Daschle, a South Dakota Democrat, told reporters.

A White House budget team was due to meet congressional negotiators on Wednesday afternoon to discuss the spending side of the budget, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said, adding there may be talks later in the day on taxes.

Speaking to reporters, McCurry scrupulously avoided criticising the tax compromise reached late on Tuesday between House and Senate Republicans, saying only: "They clearly did not write the final version of tax legislation last night."

After days of talks, House and Senate Republicans agreed on the outlines of a bill cutting taxes $85 billion over five years, fulfilling the tax portion of the May balanced-budget accord beween congressional leaders and Clinton.
Negotiators from the congressional Republicans, Democrats and the White House are trying to hammer out legislation on spending and taxes to enact that accord by early August.

The Republican agreement included several items the White House has strenuously opposed, including the indexation of capital gains for inflation that allows citizens to pay lower taxes on the rise in the value of their investment.
On another hot-button issue, Republicans proposed allowing fewer low-income working families to receive a proposed $500 per child tax credit than the administration wants.

"It is veto bait," Daschle said of this provision. "There is absolutely no way with which the president or Democrats in the Congress can support a bill that doesn't provide tax relief to those in the average incomes in this country."
McCurry, however, chose to take the high road, avoiding criticising the Republicans and arguing that their common position would not be the final outcome.
Asked if Clinton would veto the bill as worked out by the Republicans, he said: "The bill's a long way from finished.

"The only thing that's happened is that the Republicans stopped fighting amongst themselves about the tax bill but they now have to sit down and negotiate with Democratic members of Congress and also with the White House," he added.

Their efforts have been complicated by the disagreements between House and Senate Republicans and by the abortive coup launched by some House Republicans earlier this month to oust their leader, House Speaker Newt Gingrich.
Gingrich, who has been trying to get Republicans to focus on passing the budget, on Wednesday said Republicans must put the "tiresome and overwrought" saga over his leadership behind them.

The effort to balance the budget has been helped by the U.S. economy's strong growth, which has produced unexpectedly high tax revenues and shrunk the deficit to $11 billion for the first nine months of the fiscal year, which ends Sept. 30.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Wednesday it would be a "very good year" for the federal budget deficit but that no final estimate was available yet for the end of fiscal 1997.
